title: Pauri 1, meaning: the wall of falsehood
hookLine: thinking a hundred thousand times cannot reach Him; the wall of falsehood falls by walking in His order (Japji 1)

cards: Four familiar tricks for getting closer to whatever matters most. Think harder: run it through your head again. Go quiet: a retreat, the phone in a drawer.
Get more: the next purchase, the next raise will settle it. Get cleverer: one more book, one more podcast. Guru Nanak's first pauri takes tricks like these one at a time and gently closes each door.
Then it opens a different one.

teach.b: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By thinking, He can't be reached, though you think a hundred thousand times. By keeping silent, you don't become silent inside, though you sit absorbed without end.
The hunger of the hungry isn't satisfied, even by heaping up the goods of all the worlds. You may have a hundred thousand clevernesses, and not one goes with you.

Thought, silence, having, cleverness: none of them is wicked. They just can't get you there. Some readers hear the first line as ritual cleansing instead: washing a hundred thousand times won't make the mind clean.
Either way, effort alone falls short. Then the question. Kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai, kiv koorhai tutai paal?
How is the wall of falsehood torn down? Paal is a wall or a bank, the kind that walls off a field; Macauliffe renders it as a veil. Koorh is the false, the fake.
So a wall of falsehood stands between us and the true. And the answer: hukam rajaaee chalnaa, Naanak likhiaa naal.
Walk in the hukam of the One whose will it is, written, says Nanak, along with us.
Hukam runs all through Sikh life.
It means an order, a command, the way a ruler's word goes out. In Japji it's bigger: the order of things, the will running through everything, the way the world actually is.
You met a daily piece of it in camp three, the hukamnama. In the pauri, the wall doesn't come down by out-thinking it. It comes down by walking in step.

how: Sikhs recite the first pauri every morning in Japji; hukam is central to Sikh teaching, and the daily hukamnama read from the Guru Granth Sahib is received as the order for that day.

o: the order, the will running through everything
a sweet pudding handed out after the prayers
a long walk to a holy river every spring

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: the first pauri says thinking hard is wicked
thought, silence, having and cleverness aren't wicked; they just can't get you there.
the wall of falsehood falls by walking in the hukam
hukam rajaaee chalnaa: walk in the order, written along with us.
everyone reads the first line the same way
some hear thinking, others ritual cleansing; either way effort alone falls short.

games.q: the pauri asks: how do we become true, how does the wall of falsehood come down? what's its answer?
o: walk in the hukam, the order.
games.why: hukam rajaaee chalnaa: walk in the order of the One whose will it is.

practice: Pick one thing you've been turning over, a decision, a conversation, a worry, and instead of thinking about it again, set it down in front of you like a bag you've carried too far.

Feel your feet on the floor and the breath going in and out on its own; in the pauri's language, that breath is already walking in the order, without a single thought. If you pray, you can let Waheguru carry the bag for a while.

wordCard.voice: Hukam. The order, the will running through everything. Japji's first pauri says the wall of falsehood falls by walking in it.

carryVoice: Your line: walk in the order. Four doors closed, and one door opened. Until tomorrow.
